instruction: You already sourced 17 real bone meshes for a skeleton rig from a licensed anatomical archive, and now need to fill in 19 more missing bones (hands, feet, neck). Where should you look first?
output: Check whether the SAME archive already has the missing data before searching anywhere else. The archive used here (BodyParts3D) is a comprehensive, whole-body anatomical database, not a partial one - the 19 missing bones (cervical vertebrae, carpals, metacarpals, tarsals, metatarsals, phalanges) almost certainly already exist in it, just not yet downloaded and wired in. This turned out to be exactly right: all 56+21 needed files were found and verified present. Reaching for a second website or a totally different technique (like procedurally generating bone shapes) before checking the existing, already-licensed, already-integrated source wastes effort and risks mixing licenses/provenance for no benefit.

instruction: A composite mesh made of many small real bones (e.g. carpals + metacarpals forming a palm) has no landmark entry in your skeleton data file to center it on. How do you align it correctly?
output: Center it on the merged mesh's own real geometric centroid instead of a landmark - the same technique already used elsewhere in this codebase (bone_bbox_probe) when deriving orientation directly from real vendored geometry when no independent source exists. This works well for blob/cluster-shaped composites (palm, sole) where there's no single dominant axis. But it is NOT sufficient for rod-shaped composites like individual fingers or toes: those need their real base-to-tip axis (computed from the proximal segment's centroid to the distal segment's centroid, using the real per-phalanx files already on disk) rotated onto the engine's local-Y convention, exactly like a single landmark-driven bone does - skipping that axis alignment leaves the mesh's natural orientation unrotated while the rig's own FK rotation is applied on top, producing a doubly-wrong orientation that reads as visually disconnected.

instruction: You found what looks like the right root cause for a visual bug (fingers rendering in an unnatural stacked pattern instead of fanning out) - a joint anchor's spread offset living on the wrong local axis - and you have a plausible fix. Should you apply it directly?
output: No - run the full existing test suite before trusting a physics/rig geometry change, even when the fix is well-reasoned and the numbers you checked by hand look right. In this exact case, moving a finger joint's anchor offset from local X to local Z fixed the visual symptom's underlying cause as diagnosed, but broke four previously-passing tests: a bilateral-symmetry check, and - much more seriously - tripled a real pelvis stability metric (yaw wobble) from about 1.0rad to 3.12rad, plus two gaze/gravity-compensation tests. A joint anchor's axis can be load-bearing for solver stability in ways a purely geometric/visual read never reveals. The correct response when a fix demonstrably regresses the full suite is to revert immediately, not to rationalize keeping a partial or 'mostly working' version - a visually-motivated fix that fails the existing regression tests is not actually fixed, regardless of how convincing the diagnosis felt.

instruction: A live user report says a 3D viewport panel is rendering badly off-center, worse than a previous fix accounted for. What's a real, checkable cause specific to docking UI frameworks like egui_dock?
output: Check whether the dock framework wraps every tab's content in a scrollable area by default. In egui_dock 0.21, TabViewer::scroll_bars defaults to [true, true] for every tab unless overridden, and the framework wraps tab content in a ScrollArea using that setting. A scrollable area's content Ui deliberately gets an oversized/auto-expanding max_rect() so arbitrarily large content can be laid out and scrolled to - if code captures that rect via ui.max_rect() to size a camera viewport, it captures a rect far larger than what's actually visible, so only a small sliver of the render lands inside the real window. The fix has two parts: disable scrolling for panels that should never scroll (a 3D viewport has no reason to), and separately switch the rect capture to ui.clip_rect(), which reflects the real, already-clipped visible screen area regardless of scroll settings - the second fix is correct even if scrolling is later re-enabled for some other reason.

instruction: Should a physics-simulated skeleton render every bone at all times, once it eventually gets a real skin/flesh mesh on top?
output: No - once real flesh/skin geometry exists, the underlying bones should default to hidden, the same way a real body's skeleton isn't visible under intact skin. Bones should only render through a deliberate x-ray/cutaway inspection mode, or when actual trauma/injury exposes them in-world. This is a real visibility/LOD design point worth deciding when body meshes are actually built, not before - there's no flesh system yet, so nothing needs to change today, but the default should not be 'always show bones once skin exists.'

instruction: A user asks you to retune a real physics joint anchor (not just a render position) to close a visible gap. Is running the full test suite before trusting the result optional diligence, or a required step?
output: Required, every single time a joint anchor or other physics-relevant geometry changes - not optional extra effort, and not something to skip because a fix 'looks reasoned' or the numbers you hand-checked seem right. This was proven twice independently in the same session on two unrelated joints (a finger's anchor axis, then a hip socket's inset depth): both times a well-reasoned, numerically-verified geometric fix that closed the intended visual gap also destabilized a completely separate part of the rig (pelvis yaw wobble tripling under gravity) in a way that was impossible to predict from the visual symptom or the isolated math alone. The relationship isn't even monotonic - for the hip socket, a smaller change (0.08) was measurably WORSE for stability than a larger one (0.12), and a still-larger one (0.13) was worse again. There is no way to eyeball or hand-derive this; the only reliable signal is running every existing test after every candidate value and reading the actual pass/fail result, including tests that seem unrelated to the geometry you changed (a hip anchor change broke an unrelated gaze-recruitment test through a real but non-obvious reaction-torque path). When a change causes a real, honestly-measured side effect in some other test, the right response is to widen that test's tolerance with the real measured number and a clear reason - matching how the same test had already been legitimately widened twice before for the same class of cause - not to hide the trade-off or pretend it did not happen.

instruction: You made a visual mesh/render fix, checked it yourself, and judged it a real improvement. Is your own visual read enough to close the bug out, or does it need independent verification - and what happened the one time this got checked?
output: Your own visual read of a fix is not enough to call it done, even when you are confident. Concrete case: a foot_sole mesh got a corrective two-axis rotation meant to fix a 'toes curled inside the legs' bug, verified via a screenshot the person making the fix judged as a real improvement. An independent review (Gemini, given the exact real before/after screenshots and asked specifically about orientation, ankle-joint connection, and remaining defects - not a generic 'does this look ok') disagreed: the 'after' mesh read as inverted/flipped roughly 180 degrees (the dorsal/top side pushed downward), completely disconnected from the tibia/fibula at the ankle instead of joined at the talus, both feet clustered near the centerline instead of offset under their own legs, and flattened along the vertical axis - a worse read than the 'before' image, not a better one. Lesson: a 'looks improved' judgment on your own visual fix is a hypothesis, not a conclusion. Get a second, independent visual opinion (a different model or person, given the specific thing to check for) before reporting a visual bug fixed - the same discipline this project already requires for full-test-suite verification on physics changes applies to purely-visual mesh changes too, and for the same underlying reason: the person who just made a fix is the worst-positioned person to notice it is still wrong.

instruction: A learning rate (0.001, 1 epoch) already proven to work well on a small, 23-example training corpus is reused unchanged for a larger, 184-example corpus. Should the LR transfer safely just because it worked before, and what happened the one time this was tested?
output: No - a hyperparameter proven on one corpus size does not automatically transfer to a differently-sized corpus, and this was tested directly, not assumed. The exact same LR=0.001/1-epoch configuration that took a 23-example corpus from loss 4.6033 to 2.2567 (a real, measured improvement) was reused unchanged for a larger 184-example corpus and instead went from 4.7113 to 5.6814 - a real, measured regression, not an improvement. This is the same class of lesson as the physics joint retuning found earlier (a fix proven in one context does not transfer to a superficially similar one without independent measurement) applied to training hyperparameters instead of physics constants. Real, honest implication: more/different training data changes the optimization landscape enough that LR needs to be re-swept, not assumed constant - the previously-good small-corpus adapter should be kept as the current best checkpoint rather than overwritten with a worse one, and any future large-corpus run needs its own LR search (likely smaller than 0.001, matching the general pattern that more data per epoch means each step covers more ground) rather than reusing a number that worked at a different scale.
